quotes.text: Guitar was always my first love and first focus and it's something that I actually find really easy to do. But in Leppard for the last 24 years. It's not that challenging, the guitars parts you know. I'm not the only guitar player in the band. I mean Phil has been with the band ten years longer than I have. Phil's been with Def Leppard 34 years. So he obviously plays the majority of the solos because the majority of the songs that we still play in Def Leppard to this day pre date my involvement. I mean they're all the classic songs from the 80s before I was with the band.

So Phil played those solos on the records. So he absolutely is entitled to play them live you know. It would be ridiculous for him not to. So you know I don't get to play a lot of guitar in Def Leppard but I get to sing a hell of lot. So I've really been more focused on being a writer and a singer for the last 24 years.

But doing that brief tour with Lizzy in 2011 really reconnected me to my first love you know. Because here I was on stage with Scott Gorham and Brian Downey and playing Black Rose and Emerald and Jailbreak and you know Don't Believe A Word. All these great songs. Great riffs and great solos. It totally just transported me back to being 16 again in my bedroom. Just trying to really learn how to play guitar.

And this was all done around the same time that I was working on the new Def Leppard record. But no, I didn't have any ideas for this (Last In Line) that I brought across to Def Leppard. Leppard's a very, very different kind of thing.

And to be honest and just talking about that subject I actually had very little to do with this new Def Leppard record. Which is very ironic because I genuinely honestly hand on heart believe it's the best record the band has made in the 24 years I've been with Leppard. But the one I've had the least to do with. So I think the universe is trying to tell me something. You know that I should butt out of their business and just let them write the songs you know.

Well thank you. That's very charitable of you to say so actually. But it is all around it's a great Def Leppard record. Nut Leppard's a very different thing. I mean Leppard's a very diverse band. You know Last In Line does one thing. Just hard rock. Straight up hard rock. Whereas with Leppard it's not that simple. You know there's a couple of rock songs and then we gotta divert into this genre and then into that one.
It's a very multi-faceted creative process making a Def Leppard record. You know making a Last In Line record is easy peasy my comparison.

With that one, I actually worked out the melodic thing and right at the end Mutt Lange said, 'Just vibe out on the end. Play solos and licks and go around the vocal.' Because it was such a melodic, amazing, beautiful melody it was so easy to weave in and out of Joe's vocals at the end. Then the chorus is so melodic that it was so easy just to play all those licks. It kind of played itself.

Things were going too fast for me. I was still enjoying it, but I was using drink as a crutch. It wasn't nice to go out in that way, but it was something that needed to happen for them and the best thing to happen health-wise for me. If I'd stayed, there was a good chance that I'd have ended up going the same way as Steve Clark.

We'd turned up at this soundstage someplace in Battersea, in London, and there was David Mallet. Now, I didn't know who he was really, but I knew he had worked with Queen. That was good enough for me. We walked into this pre-built stage. We had nothing to do with it. We can take absolutely no credit for it.
